Chapter 4: Overcoming Procrastination and Negative Self-Talk
Even when you’ve built strong routines, there’s still a good chance you’ll run into procrastination—or that nagging voice of self-doubt. If you’ve ever set high standards for yourself, or worried about making mistakes, you know exactly what I’m talking about.
So, what’s really behind these challenges? And how can you actually move past them?
Procrastination usually pops up when anxiety, perfectionism, or fear of failure start creeping in. Think about it—when a task feels too big, or you’re not sure how it’ll turn out, it’s easy to just... avoid it. That avoidance might give you a quick sense of relief, but in the end, it usually piles on more stress.
Here’s a simple trick that really helps: break the big stuff down into tiny, doable steps. Instead of stressing over the entire project, just focus on the next thing you can actually do. It’s a lot less overwhelming, and it’s way easier to make a start. For example, if you need to write a report, forget about the whole thing for a moment. Maybe just jot down a rough outline, or set a timer for ten minutes and see how much you can get done. That first step is the hardest—but once you’re moving, it gets easier.
Now, let’s talk about negative self-talk. That’s the inner critic that keeps telling you you’re not good enough, or that you’ll mess up. Most of the time, it’s just echoing old fears or impossible expectations. But the first step to changing it... is noticing it.
Try this: imagine your negative self-talk as if it’s a video game villain or a rival character. When you hear that critical voice, ask yourself—would you actually believe that villain? Probably not! Once you see those thoughts as something outside of you, it’s easier to question them, and swap them for something more supportive. So instead of thinking, “I’ll never be good at this,” you might say, “Hey, this is new—I can get better with practice.”
Let’s run through a few quick strategies for handling procrastination and negative self-talk:
First—break big tasks into smaller, bite-sized steps.
Second—use a timer, or just tell yourself, “I’ll work on this for five minutes.” That tiny push can make a huge difference.
Third—when those unhelpful thoughts show up, treat them like they’re coming from an annoying rival. Challenge them, and replace them with something kinder.
And finally—give yourself some credit for every bit of progress, even if it’s small. Self-compassion keeps you moving forward.
When you start facing procrastination and negative self-talk head-on, you’ll notice you’re not just getting more done—you’re feeling more confident and a whole lot less stressed. These are the skills that help you keep your momentum, and actually enjoy growing and improving along the way.
